ML01.prompt: A hospital dataset contains five visits per patient. You want to predict outcomes for patients the model has never seen. Which evaluation design best matches that claim?

options.text: Shuffle all visit rows and split them randomly.
options.feedback: A patient's visits can land in both partitions, allowing patient-specific information to inflate new-patient performance.

options.text: Assign every visit from one patient to the same partition.
options.feedback: Grouping by patient prevents identity overlap and directly tests transfer to unseen patients. Feature availability still needs checking.

options.text: Train on every patient and evaluate a second time on those same visits.
options.feedback: That measures fit to observed cases, not performance on independent patients.

options.text: Randomly split rows, but remove the explicit patient ID column.
options.feedback: Other measurements can identify or strongly resemble the same patient, so removing one identifier does not remove within-patient dependence.

ML01.explanation: Choose the independent split unit from the deployment question before choosing an algorithm. New-patient and future-visit evaluation support different claims.
ML01.skill: Match the split unit to the generalization claim

ML01.prompt: Training targets are 2, 4 and 9. A squared-error baseline predicts their training mean for every new case. On independent targets 3 and 7, what are its mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), in squared target units and target units respectively?

options.text: MSE 2; MAE 4.
options.feedback: This swaps the role of squared and absolute errors: the absolute errors are both 2, while their squares are both 4.

options.text: MSE 8; MAE 4.
options.feedback: Those are sums across two cases; both requested metrics divide by the number of evaluated cases.

options.text: MSE 5; MAE 2.
options.feedback: Five is the training mean and hence the prediction, not the mean squared evaluation error.

options.text: MSE 4; MAE 2.
options.feedback: The prediction is 5. Its errors are +2 and −2, giving MSE (4+4)/2=4 and MAE (2+2)/2=2.

ML01.explanation: The fitting objective determines the baseline. Use only training targets to choose its constant, then calculate error on separate evaluation targets.
ML01.skill: Calculate and evaluate a constant baseline

ML02.prompt: You will compare classifiers using five-fold cross-validation. Your pipeline fills missing values, standardizes numeric features and selects features using training labels. Where should these operations be fitted?

options.text: Fit them once on the full dataset before constructing folds.
options.feedback: Both held-out values and, for feature selection, held-out labels would influence the representation used to evaluate each fold.

options.text: Fit them on each validation fold because that is where scores are measured.
options.feedback: Validation data must receive the training-fitted transformation; fitting on it changes the evaluation procedure and leaks information.

options.text: Fit the complete pipeline separately on each fold's training portion.
options.feedback: Each fold's fitted preprocessing and feature selection then use only the data allowed for training that fold.

options.text: Fit scaling on all rows, but put only the classifier inside cross-validation.
options.feedback: Even label-free scaling learns statistics from rows. A clean independent-fold protocol fits it inside the training boundary too.

ML02.explanation: Learned preprocessing is part of the estimator. Cross-validation must repeat the entire fitted pipeline, not only its last classifier.

ML02.prompt: A feature's training mean is 10 and its training standard deviation is 2. The fitted standardizer uses z=(x−mean)/standard deviation. What should it output for a validation value of 14?

options.text: 2, using the saved training statistics.
options.feedback: The held-out value becomes (14−10)/2=2. No validation-fitted statistics are needed.

options.text: 7, because standardization divides 14 by 2.
options.feedback: Standardization also subtracts the training mean; ignoring centering computes a different transformation.

options.text: 0, by centering the single validation value on itself.
options.feedback: Re-fitting on a one-case validation set changes the transformation and removes the intended training reference.

options.text: 4, because 14−10=4.
options.feedback: Four is the centered value, but standardization additionally divides it by the nonzero training standard deviation.

ML02.explanation: Apply exactly the same learned transformation to future data. The resulting z value is measured in training-standard-deviation units.

ML03.prompt: Two input columns are nearly copies of one another. A least-squares model predicts well, but its individual coefficients change sharply under small data changes. What is the most defensible interpretation?

options.text: Collinearity can make individual coefficients unstable even when combined predictions remain similar.
options.feedback: Several coefficient combinations can explain nearly the same signal. Inspect conditioning and consider a regularized, validated fit.

options.text: The model has proved that both columns have independent causal effects.
options.feedback: Predictive coefficients from observational data do not establish intervention effects, especially when features carry overlapping information.

options.text: Low prediction error means every coefficient is uniquely and reliably identified.
options.feedback: Prediction quality and parameter identifiability are different questions; redundant directions can leave coefficients poorly determined.

options.text: Explicitly inverting the normal-equation matrix will remove the instability.
options.feedback: An explicit inverse does not fix collinearity and can worsen numerical problems. Stable solvers and appropriate regularization address different aspects.

ML03.explanation: A stable prediction is not automatically a stable interpretation. Separate numerical conditioning, regularization and causal claims.
ML03.skill: Distinguish predictive fit from coefficient interpretation

ML03.prompt: For the diagram's no-intercept ridge model, XᵀX=14 and Xᵀy=11. The objective is summed squared error plus λw². With λ=1, what slope is fitted and what happens when λ increases?

options.text: w=11/13; a larger penalty increases its magnitude.
options.feedback: The penalty adds to XᵀX in the normal equation. Subtracting it gives the wrong direction of shrinkage.

options.text: w=11/14; the penalty cannot change the fitted coefficient.
options.feedback: This is the unregularized slope and ignores the declared λw² term.

options.text: w=11/15; a larger penalty shrinks this slope toward zero.
options.feedback: The stationary equation is (14+λ)w=11. At λ=1 the slope is 11/15; increasing this nonnegative penalty enlarges the denominator.

options.text: w=15/11; a larger penalty guarantees better test predictions.
options.feedback: This inverts the slope formula. Regularization also does not guarantee improved test error; choose it using development data.

ML03.explanation: Separate fitting from evaluation: the penalty changes the solution to the declared objective; held-out data determine whether that change helps prediction.
ML03.skill: Interpret the ridge fit and shrinkage

ML04.prompt: A trained binary classifier outputs spam probability 0.8 for a message. You change the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 without fitting again. What changed?

options.text: The predicted probability becomes 0.9.
options.feedback: A threshold is a decision rule applied to a probability; it does not replace that probability with its own value.

options.text: The model learned a different feature representation.
options.feedback: No optimization or feature transformation was run. The fitted representation remains unchanged.

options.text: The probability is now guaranteed to be calibrated.
options.feedback: Calibration concerns confidence versus observed frequencies. Changing one cutoff does not establish calibration.

options.text: The decision changes from spam to not spam, while the probability stays 0.8.
options.feedback: The same score exceeds 0.5 but not 0.9. This changes the decision, not the fitted parameters.

ML04.explanation: Separate fitting, probability prediction and decision-making. Select thresholds on development data using the relevant trade-off, not the final test.

ML04.prompt: A three-class softmax model outputs probabilities [0.7, 0.2, 0.1]. The true class is the second entry. For cross-entropy with natural logarithms and one hard target, which vector is the derivative with respect to the three logits?

options.feedback: This keeps the probabilities but omits subtraction of the one-hot target from the true-class entry.
The softmax-cross-entropy derivative is probability minus one-hot target: [0.7,0.2−1,0.1].
This is the negative gradient. It describes the descent direction before multiplying by a positive learning rate, not the requested derivative.
This drops how the softmax normalization couples all three scores. Incorrect-class logits also receive derivatives.

ML04.explanation: For a hard multiclass target, dL/dz equals p−one_hot(y). A descent step tends to raise the true-class logit and lower the others.

ML05.prompt: You tried 100 hyperparameter settings and chose the one with the highest final-test score. You then bootstrap those test rows and obtain a narrow interval. What remains wrong with the final performance claim?

options.text: Bootstrapping requires every sampled row to appear exactly once.
options.feedback: Ordinary bootstrap samples deliberately allow repeated rows. That is not the selection problem here.

options.text: The test set influenced selection; resampling it does not undo that selection bias.
options.feedback: The winner was chosen partly for fitting test noise. Use a fresh independent assessment or a protocol that nests selection inside evaluation.

options.text: Trying more settings automatically makes the test estimate unbiased.
options.feedback: More candidates create more chances to exploit test noise, rather than restoring independence.

options.text: The result becomes independent if the winning model has fewer parameters.
options.feedback: Model size does not reverse information already used during selection. The evaluation boundary was still crossed.

ML05.explanation: Selecting a model is itself learning. An uncertainty interval for a selected fixed prediction set is not a correction for choosing that prediction set using the test.
ML05.skill: Identify selection bias beyond interval width

ML05.prompt: An objective adds the L2 penalty λw²/2 to its data loss. For one coefficient w=3 and λ=0.2, what loss contribution and derivative with respect to w come from this penalty alone?

options.text: Loss 0.6; derivative 0.2.
options.feedback: This resembles an absolute-value penalty calculation. Squared L2 uses w² in the loss and λw in its derivative.

options.text: Loss 1.8; derivative 1.2.
options.feedback: These values omit the stated division by 2, doubling both the penalty and its derivative.

options.text: Loss 0.9; derivative 1.8.
options.feedback: The loss is correct, but the derivative of λw²/2 is λw, not λw².

options.text: Loss 0.9; derivative 0.6.
options.feedback: The penalty is 0.2×9/2=0.9; differentiating gives 0.2×3=0.6.

ML05.explanation: Keep the objective's normalization explicit. Libraries using a different loss or penalty scaling can require different numerical regularization settings.

ML06.prompt: A k-nearest-neighbours classifier compares an income feature measured in thousands with another numeric feature whose useful differences are around 0.01. Income dominates Euclidean distance. What is the most useful first controlled comparison?

options.text: Increase k until the smaller feature starts using larger units.
options.feedback: Changing the number of neighbours does not change feature units or directly repair the distance geometry.

options.text: Standardize all rows together before splitting so both partitions use their own information.
options.feedback: The representation should be learned on training data, not from the final holdout being used to assess it.

options.text: Compare justified training-fitted scaling with no scaling, using the same split and neighbour rule.
options.feedback: This isolates the representation's effect on distance while preserving an independent evaluation boundary.

options.text: Switch to an RBF kernel without checking scales, because kernels ignore feature units.
options.feedback: RBF similarities depend on squared distances, so inappropriate feature scales can dominate kernels too.

ML06.explanation: Geometry comes before voting. Scaling is an experimentally testable choice, not a guarantee that a particular classifier will win.

ML06.prompt: A query's three neighbours have labels [A,A,B] at nonzero distances [2,2,0.2]. The classifier sums inverse-distance weights 1/d separately for each class. Which class wins, and with what class weight totals?

options.text: B wins: A has total weight 1 and B has total weight 5.
options.feedback: A receives 1/2+1/2=1, while B receives 1/0.2=5. The closest neighbour outweighs the two distant ones.

options.text: A wins: it has two neighbours and B has one.
options.feedback: That is the unweighted majority rule; the question explicitly uses inverse-distance weights.

options.text: A wins: A has total weight 4 and B has total weight 0.2.
options.feedback: This sums distances rather than inverse distances, incorrectly rewarding farther neighbours.

options.text: It is tied because each class gets normalized separately to one.
options.feedback: Normalizing separately within each class would destroy the comparison. The specified method sums the original neighbour weights.

ML06.explanation: The same neighbours can produce different decisions under uniform and distance-weighted voting. The weighting rule is part of the model specification.

ML07.prompt: A naive Bayes spam classifier orders messages usefully, but two highly correlated indicator features make it excessively confident. Which explanation best fits?

options.text: Its conditional-independence assumption can count overlapping evidence too strongly even when class ordering is useful.
options.feedback: Useful classification and reliable probability values are different properties. Correlated evidence can damage the latter without destroying the former.

options.text: Good classification accuracy mathematically guarantees calibrated probabilities.
options.feedback: Accuracy uses decisions and can remain unchanged when probabilities become much more extreme and poorly calibrated.

options.text: The method requires features to be independent across the entire dataset, not within classes.
options.feedback: Naive Bayes factorizes features conditional on the class. Overall feature independence is a different statement.

options.text: A larger smoothing value removes every form of feature dependence.
options.feedback: Smoothing changes likelihood estimates and avoids zero probabilities; it does not make correlated observations conditionally independent.

ML07.explanation: Test probability quality separately from ranking and classification. A modelling assumption can be adequate for a decision yet poor for confidence estimation.
ML07.skill: Separate naive Bayes decisions from calibration

ML07.prompt: For two observed binary indicators, assume conditional independence given class. Spam has prior 0.2 and indicator likelihoods 0.6 and 0.5. Ham has prior 0.8 and likelihoods 0.1 and 0.2. What is the normalized spam probability under this model?

options.feedback: This is the unnormalized spam score 0.2×0.6×0.5. It still must be divided by the sum of both class scores.
This is only the spam prior; it ignores the observed indicators' likelihoods.

options.text: Approximately 0.7895
options.feedback: Spam scores 0.06 and ham scores 0.016. Normalizing gives 0.06/(0.06+0.016)=0.78947…

options.text: Approximately 0.9375
options.feedback: That normalizes only the class-conditional products 0.30 and 0.02, omitting the unequal class priors.

ML07.explanation: Multiply each class's prior by its conditional feature likelihoods, then normalize across classes. The result is conditional on the model assumptions, not an empirical calibration guarantee.

ML08.prompt: A random forest reaches almost perfect held-out accuracy. You discover that one input is a copy of the target. Would growing more trees make the experiment trustworthy?

options.text: Yes, because averaging more trees removes target leakage.
options.feedback: Averaging reduces some estimator variation; it does not remove information that should never be available at prediction time.

options.text: Yes, if each tree uses a bootstrap sample.
options.feedback: Bootstrap sampling still gives fitted trees access to the leaked target feature. Resampling is not a leakage barrier.

options.text: Only if the copied target receives low feature importance.
options.feedback: An importance diagnostic does not legalize a forbidden feature, and importance values can be misleading with correlated inputs.

options.text: No; remove the forbidden feature and rebuild the clean training and evaluation pipeline.
options.feedback: The task was easier than the intended deployment problem. Re-evaluation after the correction is required, regardless of ensemble size.

ML08.explanation: More trees create neither new independent data nor protection against invalid features. Validate the information boundary before interpreting a high score.
ML08.skill: Recognize leakage that ensembles cannot repair

ML08.prompt: A classification tree node contains four positives and four negatives. A split creates two four-case children with class counts [3,1] and [1,3]. Using Gini=1−sum(class proportion²), what is the parent-minus-weighted-children impurity gain?

options.feedback: This is each child's impurity, and also their weighted average here. Gain subtracts that value from the parent's impurity.
Parent Gini is 0.5; each child has 1−0.75²−0.25²=0.375. The gain is 0.5−0.375=0.125.
That would require pure children with zero impurity. Both children here still contain both classes.
This results from subtracting the sum of the two child impurities without weighting by their sample fractions.

ML08.explanation: Weight each child impurity by its share of cases. A positive training gain is only a local fitting improvement, not proof of better generalization.
ML08.skill: Calculate a sample-weighted tree split gain

ML09.prompt: You want to learn a stacking model that combines several classifiers. Which training inputs should the stacker receive for each training row?

options.text: Predictions from base models trained on that same row and its label.
options.feedback: In-sample predictions can be unrealistically easy, teaching the stacker a relationship that will not hold for unseen cases.

options.text: Out-of-fold predictions from base models that did not train on that row.
options.feedback: These inputs better represent how base models behave on unseen rows. Keep a separate final evaluation beyond the complete stacking procedure.

options.text: The final test labels, so the stacker can learn the best mixture weights.
options.feedback: This directly uses assessment answers for learning and removes the final test's independence.

options.text: Only the base models' aggregate training accuracies, with no row-level predictions.
options.feedback: An overall accuracy does not supply the example-specific signals a predictive stacker is meant to combine.

ML09.explanation: The combining model needs an honest view of its inputs' generalization errors. Out-of-fold generation is part of the complete fitted protocol.

ML09.prompt: For squared-error regression, targets are [3,7] and current predictions are [2,5]. A fitted correction predicts their residuals [1,2]. With additive update new=old+0.1×correction, what are the new predictions and their mean squared error?

options.text: [3,7] and MSE 0
options.feedback: This applies the full correction at rate 1. The specified shrinkage rate is 0.1.
These subtract the residual correction instead of adding it, moving the predictions away from the targets.
The predictions are right, but 2.5 is the old MSE. Recalculate error after the update.
Residuals become [0.9,1.8]. Their mean squared error is (0.81+3.24)/2=2.025.

ML09.explanation: Shrinkage scales each learner's contribution. This illustrative training improvement does not imply that every boosting round improves validation performance.

ML10.prompt: Two classifiers have saved predictions on the same 500 independent test cases. You want a bootstrap interval for their accuracy difference, conditional on these fixed fitted models. How should each replicate be formed?

options.text: Resample different test indices independently for each model.
options.feedback: That discards case pairing and adds irrelevant case-composition differences to the comparison.

options.text: Shuffle each model's predictions so the cases are independent.
options.feedback: Shuffling predictions breaks their alignment with the true labels and no longer evaluates the saved systems.

options.text: Sample 500 case indices with replacement once and evaluate both models on those same sampled indices.
options.feedback: Shared sampled cases preserve pairing, so each replicate measures the difference on the same resampled evaluation units.

options.text: Use only the two final accuracy values and resample those numbers.
options.feedback: Two aggregate scores omit per-case outcomes and their pairing; they cannot recreate this case-level resampling distribution.

ML10.explanation: This procedure measures conditional test-sample variability. It does not include retraining, model-selection uncertainty or arbitrary deployment shift; dependent cases require an appropriate grouped design.
ML10.skill: Preserve pairing and state bootstrap scope

ML10.prompt: You multiply binary logits by a positive constant and then apply sigmoid. In this example no score crosses probability 0.5. Which quantities can change despite identical class decisions and score ranking?

options.text: Log loss and Brier score can change; accuracy and ROC-AUC stay fixed here.
options.feedback: Probability-sensitive losses read the changed numbers, while accuracy reads unchanged decisions and AUC reads unchanged ordering.

options.text: Accuracy must increase because the model sounds more confident.
options.feedback: The decisions are identical. Greater confidence is not evidence of more correct predictions.

options.text: ROC-AUC must improve because the positive logits grew.
options.feedback: Positive scaling preserves score ordering, so pairwise discrimination and ROC-AUC are unchanged in this example.

options.text: No metric can change if the predicted labels are unchanged.
options.feedback: Hard labels discard confidence information. Log loss and Brier score still evaluate the probabilities assigned to actual labels.

ML10.explanation: Distinguish decisions, ranking and probability quality. They are separate evaluation objects even when computed from the same cases.
ML10.skill: Separate calibration-sensitive losses from classification and ranking scores

ML11.prompt: You try several scalers and cluster counts, then choose the configuration with the best agreement with known species labels. The clustering fit itself never receives labels. How should you describe the full selection procedure?

options.text: The clustering fit was unsupervised, but choosing settings by label agreement introduced supervised guidance.
options.feedback: Labels affected which representation and settings were selected, even though the clustering algorithm's internal fit did not consume them.

options.text: It was completely label-free because labels were absent from the fit method.
options.feedback: The information boundary includes selection decisions, not only the fit function's arguments.

options.text: The selected clusters prove that species are the only natural grouping.
options.feedback: Selecting for agreement favours that known partition; it does not establish a unique natural grouping of the features.

options.text: Any use of labels makes the fitted model a supervised classifier with a class-probability head.
options.feedback: The selected model can remain a clustering model; the issue is supervision in the overall procedure, not an automatic architectural change.

ML11.explanation: Describe fitting and selection separately. Labels can support a clearly labelled post-hoc diagnostic, but using that diagnostic to choose settings changes the learning protocol.
ML11.skill: Distinguish unsupervised fitting from supervised selection

ML11.prompt: One Gaussian-mixture component has responsibilities [0.8,0.2] for scalar observations [0,2]. In the EM mean update, use mean=sum(responsibility×value)/sum(responsibility). What is this component's updated mean?

options.feedback: That is the unweighted mean of the two observations and ignores the component's unequal responsibilities.
This divides the weighted sum by the number of observations. EM divides by the sum of this component's responsibilities, which is 1.
The weighted sum is 0.8×0+0.2×2=0.4, and total responsibility is 0.8+0.2=1, so the updated mean is 0.4.
That would use reversed responsibilities [0.2,0.8], giving the second point most of the weight.

ML11.explanation: Soft responsibilities let a point contribute fractionally to several components. The effective component population is its responsibility sum, not the total row count.

ML12.prompt: PCA retains 99% of input variance, yet a classifier loses accuracy after reduction. Which explanation is consistent with what PCA optimizes?

options.text: Retaining 99% variance guarantees retaining at least 99% classification accuracy.
options.feedback: Explained input variance is not an accuracy guarantee and contains no direct statement about target relevance.

options.text: PCA must have accidentally trained on test labels.
options.feedback: Accuracy can drop even with a clean, label-free PCA fit because its reconstruction objective is different from classification.

options.text: Whitening would recover all information removed by discarded components.
options.feedback: Whitening rescales retained coordinates; it does not reconstruct information discarded with other directions.

options.text: A low-variance direction may carry useful label information that PCA discarded.
options.feedback: PCA prioritizes input variance, not predictive signal. Evaluate downstream quality separately from reconstruction or variance retained.

ML12.explanation: Compression quality and task quality answer different questions. Compare reduction choices inside the training/selection boundary, keeping the final evaluation independent.
ML12.skill: Distinguish variance preservation from target usefulness

ML12.prompt: Centered two-feature data have population covariance diag(9,1), in fixed original units. PCA keeps only the first principal direction. What variance fraction is retained, and what is the expected squared reconstruction error averaged across both features per row?

options.text: 90% retained; mean-per-feature error 1.
options.feedback: The retained fraction is right. The discarded direction contributes total error 1 per row, which becomes 0.5 when averaged across two features.

options.text: 90% retained; mean-per-feature error 0.5.
options.feedback: The retained fraction is 9/(9+1)=0.9. Discarded variance is 1 per row, divided by two feature coordinates for mean-per-feature error.

options.text: 50% retained; mean-per-feature error 0.5.
options.feedback: Keeping one of two dimensions does not mean retaining half the variance; their variances are unequal.

options.text: 100% retained; mean-per-feature error 0.
options.feedback: The discarded direction has nonzero variance 1, so it contains variation that cannot be reconstructed from the retained direction.

ML12.explanation: State the coordinate system and averaging convention. Standardizing the two original features would change their covariance and this variance calculation.
ML12.skill: Compute PCA variance and reconstruction units

ML13.prompt: You forecast tomorrow's demand using the weather that was actually measured tomorrow. At prediction time, only today's history and tomorrow's weather forecast are available. What is wrong with the evaluation?

options.text: Nothing: future weather is allowed because it is not the demand target.
options.feedback: Leakage depends on availability at prediction time, not only on whether a variable is named as the target.

options.text: It uses target-time information that the deployed forecaster would not know.
options.feedback: Replace observed future weather with genuinely available forecasts or a clearly defined separate weather-prediction pipeline, then evaluate chronologically.

options.text: It is repaired by increasing the model's sequence length.
options.feedback: More history does not make a future observation available at the forecast origin.

options.text: It is repaired by scaling tomorrow's measured weather using training statistics.
options.feedback: Training-only scaling is good practice, but it cannot legalize a feature unavailable when the prediction is made.

ML13.explanation: A forecasting feature has both a value and an information timestamp. Match every input to the declared forecast origin and horizon.

ML13.prompt: An hourly series has seasonal period 24. At the end of hour t, a seasonal-naive model forecasts hour t+1 using the same hour from the previous day. That historical count was 120 and the later observed count is 150. Which input index and absolute error are correct?

options.text: Use y(t−24); absolute error 30.
options.feedback: The error is correct for a prediction of 120, but the matching hour for target t+1 is (t+1)−24=t−23.

options.text: Use y(t+1); absolute error 0.
options.feedback: That uses the future answer itself. It is not available at origin t.

options.text: Use y(t−23); absolute error −30.
options.feedback: The input index is right, but an absolute error cannot be negative: |120−150|=30.

options.text: Use y(t−23); absolute error 30.
options.feedback: The seasonal reference is y((t+1)−24)=y(t−23), and |120−150|=30 rentals.

ML13.explanation: Define the target timestamp first, then move back one seasonal period. Off-by-one errors in lag construction can change the task or leak information.
ML13.skill: Align a seasonal baseline with its forecast horizon

ML14.prompt: A recommender log records ratings only for items the old system displayed. You treat every unshown item as disliked and evaluate a new ranking model on that table. What is the main problem?

options.text: The dot product of user and item embeddings is mathematically undefined.
options.feedback: Embedding scores can be computed. The problem is the meaning and selection of the observed feedback, not the dot product.

options.text: A deeper model automatically removes the old system's exposure bias.
options.feedback: More model capacity does not create feedback for items people never saw or justify labelling those items as disliked.

options.text: Exposure selected which preferences could be observed; missing feedback is not automatically a negative preference.
options.feedback: The old policy shaped the data. Evaluation or counterfactual claims must account for that selection rather than assuming random exposure.

options.text: Randomly shuffling the observed rows recovers ratings for unshown items.
options.feedback: Shuffling changes order, not which outcomes were ever observed. The missing counterfactual feedback remains missing.

ML14.explanation: Observed interactions combine preference with a historical exposure policy. Distinguish offline ranking performance on logged data from claims about a new policy's reward.
ML14.skill: Recognize selective feedback and exposure bias

ML14.prompt: A two-step episode yields reward 1 immediately after the current action and reward 2 at the next step. With discount γ=0.5 and return G=r1+γr2, what is the return?

options.feedback: The immediate reward is undiscounted: 1+0.5×2=2.
This sums rewards without applying the stated discount to the second reward.
This discounts both rewards by 0.5. The first reward has factor γ⁰=1 under the stated return definition.
This ignores the future reward, which still contributes 0.5×2=1.

ML14.explanation: Discounting specifies how future rewards contribute. Unlike a single-row supervised label, a sequential decision can affect later rewards and states.

ML15.prompt: A Gaussian process fitted with a smooth kernel gives narrow uncertainty bands in a new region, but the true process changes abruptly there. Which statement is most defensible?

options.text: Its uncertainty is conditional on the kernel and noise assumptions, so it can be confidently wrong when those assumptions fail.
options.feedback: A posterior quantifies uncertainty within a model. It does not automatically cover every type of distribution shift or structural misspecification.

options.text: A narrow posterior band proves there is no distribution shift.
options.feedback: The model can be certain under a wrong smoothness assumption; narrowness is not a test that the deployment distribution matches training.

options.text: The band is identical to a bootstrap interval for a fixed classifier's accuracy.
options.feedback: A function-value posterior and conditional test-sample variability concern different quantities and rely on different procedures.

options.text: Doubling the number of optimization steps guarantees coverage of the abrupt change.
options.feedback: Better optimization of a misspecified model does not by itself supply the missing structural assumption or observations.

ML15.explanation: State which uncertainty a method represents and which assumptions support it. A probabilistic model is not a distribution-free safety guarantee.

ML15.prompt: Consider a one-observation Gaussian process with zero prior mean. At the same input, prior latent variance is 1, observation-noise variance is 0.25, and observed y=2. Using posterior mean=y/(1+0.25) and latent variance=1−1/(1+0.25), what are the mean and latent variance?

options.text: Mean 2; latent variance 0.
options.feedback: These would describe noiseless interpolation. The stated positive observation noise prevents treating the measurement as exact.

options.text: Mean 1.6; latent variance 0.45.
options.feedback: 1.6 is correct, but 0.45 adds observation noise to the latent variance. That is the variance for a future noisy observation, not the latent value.

options.text: Mean 1.6; latent variance 0.2.
options.feedback: The denominator is 1.25. Mean=2/1.25=1.6 and latent variance=1−1/1.25=0.2.

options.text: Mean 2.5; latent variance −0.25.
options.feedback: This multiplies instead of solving by 1.25. A negative variance is also a warning that the conditioning calculation is wrong.

ML15.explanation: Observation noise shrinks the posterior mean toward its prior and leaves latent uncertainty. Predicting a noisy observation requires adding its noise variance separately.
ML15.skill: Calculate and interpret a one-point GP posterior

ML16.prompt: You want to deploy a classifier trained on scaled numeric inputs with a fixed feature order and label mapping. What should its inference artifact preserve?

options.text: Only the final accuracy; future inputs can reconstruct the model from that score.
options.feedback: An aggregate score does not contain model parameters, preprocessing statistics, feature ordering or label meanings.

options.text: Only the classifier weights; re-fit the scaler on every new prediction batch.
options.feedback: New-batch fitting changes the learned representation and can make identical cases receive different inputs from those used in training.

options.text: A screenshot of the training curve and the class names in any order.
options.feedback: A plot is not an executable fitted pipeline, and changing class order can silently change how predictions are interpreted.

options.text: The fitted preprocessing and estimator, feature schema, label mapping and reproducibility metadata.
options.feedback: These preserve the actual input-to-output procedure. Load only trusted, validated artifacts; some serialization formats can execute code.

ML16.explanation: The fitted model includes every learned transformation and semantic convention. Hashes help detect changed bytes, but do not establish trust or experimental fairness.
ML16.skill: Package the complete inference and experiment contract

ML16.prompt: On the same evaluation cases and target units, a baseline has mean absolute error 0.60 and a candidate has 0.57. Define delta=candidate minus baseline and relative error reduction=(baseline−candidate)/baseline. Which report is correct?

options.text: Delta +0.03 target units; relative reduction 5%.
options.feedback: The reduction percentage is right, but candidate minus baseline is 0.57−0.60=−0.03. Smaller MAE is better.

options.text: Delta −0.03 target units; relative reduction 5%.
options.feedback: The absolute difference is −0.03, and the reduction is 0.03/0.60=0.05, or 5%.

options.text: Delta −0.03 target units; relative reduction 3%.
options.feedback: 0.03 is an absolute difference in target units, not a percentage; relative reduction divides it by the baseline error.

options.text: Delta −0.03 target units; relative reduction about 5.26%.
options.feedback: About 5.26% uses the candidate error 0.57 as denominator. The stated reduction convention uses the baseline 0.60.

ML16.explanation: Define sign, units and denominator before presenting gains. Whether a small improvement justifies more complexity also depends on paired uncertainty and measured deployment cost.
ML16.skill: Report matched effects without mixing absolute and relative gains
